1254.title: Zen, closed
1254.hook: posture, poem, platform, ox, koan, bowl
1254.howItsDone: In Zen communities, zazen, seated meditation, is the center of practice; in the Soto school, the practice Dogen called shikantaza, just sitting, is sitting without a koan or other object.

segments.voice: Yesterday, what Zen is not: not just calm, not just paradox, but precepts, ritual and community. Your line: more than calm. Today the Zen block closes.

Six things on a table. A round cushion. A sheet of paper with a verse brushed on it. A raised wooden seat where a teacher once spoke. A small painting of an ox. A slip of paper with a question on it. And an empty bowl. Each opened a door in these weeks of Zen and Chan. Today they sit side by side, and then we do the one thing all six keep pointing back to. Today's word, one last time in this block: Zen.
screen: `SIX THINGS ON A TABLE.` → `CUSHION, VERSE, SEAT, OX, QUESTION, BOWL.` → `ZEN.`

segments.voice: Start with the cushion and the verse. The cushion is posture: back upright, hands resting together, eyes lowered, breath allowed to be itself. The verse is the old story of a poem on a monastery wall, answered by Huineng, a worker pounding rice in the back who could not read. Then the seat and the ox. The seat is the platform where Huineng taught, and the sutra named after it: the nature to wake up is already here, not far off. The ox is the set of pictures where a herdsman searches for an ox, finds it, tames it, rides it home, forgets it, and walks back into the market with open hands. Then the question and the bowl. The question is the koan: Zhaozhou's no, three pounds of flax, the cypress, the stone bridge, a question you live with, not one you solve over coffee. The bowl is the formal meal: bowls nested one in the next, just enough, every bowl cleaned. The ordinary task is the practice. Last, what holds all six. Each comes back to the cushion. The Japanese teacher Dogen called it shikantaza, just sitting: not sitting to get calm or to crack a koan, but sitting as the whole of it. Tomorrow a very different door opens, with a vow, a name and a land of light.
screen: `THE CUSHION AND THE VERSE.` · `THE SEAT AND THE OX.` · `THE QUESTION AND THE BOWL.` · `ALL SIX COME BACK TO SITTING.` · then, large: `JUST SIT.`

segments.voice: Sit: back upright, hands resting together, eyes lowered or closed, with no koan, no counting, no picture to hold. When a thought comes, let it be there and let it go, the way a cloud crosses a window.
Zen. The Japanese name of the school called Chan in China: posture, verse, platform, ox, koan and bowl, and under all of them, sitting. Today's word.
Your line: just sit. The block ends where it began, on the cushion. Until tomorrow.

1255.title: The Pure Land
1255.hook: the "land of bliss" of Amitabha Buddha, a path practiced widely across East Asia
1255.howItsDone: Pure Land Buddhists in China, Japan, Korea, Vietnam and beyond chant the short and long sutras on Sukhavati, call the name of Amitabha Buddha, and hope to be born in his land of bliss, where awakening is said to come without turning back.

segments.voice: Yesterday the Zen block closed where it began, on the cushion. Your line: just sit. Today, a new block.

The Buddha is staying in a grove near the city of Shravasti, with a great gathering of monks. He turns to his disciple Shariputra and describes a world. Far to the west, he says, past a great many Buddha-worlds, there's a land where a Buddha lives and teaches right now. In that land, nobody suffers, in body or in mind. The sutra goes on to fill it with jeweled trees and lotus ponds. For the coming weeks, this path stays in that land. Its name is today's word: Sukhavati.
screen: `A GROVE NEAR SHRAVASTI.` → `FAR TO THE WEST.` → `SUKHAVATI.`

segments.voice: Back on day nine hundred ninety-two, Honen taught calling Amida's name. Now, the land that name points to. First, the name. Sukhavati is Sanskrit, usually given in English as the land of bliss, or the happy land. The short sutra explains it better than any dictionary: the beings there know no pain of body and no pain of mind, only causes of joy. Second, whose land it is. The sutra says a Buddha named Amitabha lives and teaches there now. How that land came to be is a story of its own, and it starts tomorrow. Third, a detail worth keeping: the land of bliss isn't a place to retire. In the sutra, those born there don't turn back from the path to awakening. The jeweled trees and lotus ponds aren't a reward for being finished. They're the conditions that make the rest of the path easy: a Buddha nearby, the teaching in the air, nothing pulling anyone backward. A land built for waking up. Fourth, where you meet it. In China, Japan, Korea and Vietnam, Pure Land practice lives in great temples and small home altars, at morning chanting and at the bedside of the dying. Some Pure Land Buddhists sit in meditation too; others devote themselves to calling the Buddha's name. In Japanese the land is often called Gokuraku; in Chinese, Jile.
screen: `SUKHAVATI: THE LAND OF BLISS.` · `NO PAIN OF BODY OR MIND.` · `A LAND BUILT FOR WAKING UP.` · `IN TEMPLES AND HOME ALTARS.` · then, large: `THE LAND OF BLISS.`

segments.voice: Call up a peaceful place you've really known, a porch, a lake, a kitchen early in the morning, and let it come in detail: the light, the sound, the air. Then ask gently what about this place makes it easy to be kind, or clear, or awake, and stay there with your breath, letting that ease spread.

1256.title: The monk Dharmakara
1256.hook: a monk in the distant past makes his vows to create a land where all can awaken (Larger Sukhavati-vyuha)
1256.howItsDone: Pure Land Buddhists chant and study the longer sutra on the land of bliss, in which the monk Dharmakara makes his vows; in East Asia the vows are counted as forty-eight, and temples and teachers return to them often.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sukhavati: the land of bliss, far to the west, where nobody turns back from the path. Your line: the land of bliss.

A king sits in a crowd, listening to a Buddha teach. It's a story the Buddha tells his attendant Ananda in the longer sutra on the land of bliss, set in ages so far back the sutra stacks one past age on another to reach it. The Buddha teaching is named Lokeshvararaja. The king hears him, and something lands so deep that he gives up his throne, takes the robe, and becomes a monk. His new name is Dharmakara. And this monk is about to ask for something enormous.
screen: `A KING IN THE CROWD.` → `HE GIVES UP THE THRONE.` → `THE MONK DHARMAKARA.`

segments.voice: First, the change. A king becomes a monk, and that's the whole pattern in miniature: giving up one kind of power to take on another kind of work. Second, the request. Dharmakara asks his teacher to show him the lands of the Buddhas, the fine and the poor, so he can make a land of his own that gathers up what's best. His teacher shows him. Then the monk goes quiet, and in the sutra he spends an immense stretch of time thinking it through before he says a word. Third, the vows. He comes back and speaks them aloud, one by one, and they share one shape. When I become a Buddha, if my land still holds realms of suffering, may I not attain perfect awakening. When I become a Buddha, if the beings born there don't reach awakening, may I not attain it either. If not, not me. In the version of the sutra read in China and Japan, there are forty-eight. Fourth, why the shape matters. The usual bargain says: first I'll get mine, then I'll help. Dharmakara's vows run the other way, tying his own awakening to everyone else's. He refuses to count himself finished while the land he promised isn't real. The sutra says the vows were fulfilled: he became a Buddha, and his land is the land of bliss. Who he became gets a day of its own.
screen: `A KING BECOMES A MONK.` · `SHOW ME THE LANDS.` · `IF NOT, MAY I NOT AWAKEN.` · `HIS AWAKENING TIED TO EVERYONE'S.` · then, large: `FORTY-EIGHT VOWS.`

segments.voice: Choose one small, concrete thing you'll do for someone else this week, a call, a ride, a meal, an hour of listening, and give it Dharmakara's shape in your own words: I won't call this week finished until it's done. Say it once, silently, then breathe and let it settle, not as pressure but as a promise you've chosen.
The monk Dharmakara: a king who became a monk, studied the lands of the Buddhas, and vowed not to accept awakening unless his land would carry others to it. Today's word.
Your line: forty-eight vows. Each one ends the same way: if not, not me. Same time tomorrow.

1257.title: Dharmakara's primal vow
1257.hook: the vow that anyone who calls his name with faith will be born in his land
1257.carry: the door is open: trust and the name
1257.howItsDone: Pure Land Buddhists in East Asia treat this vow, hongan in Japanese, as the heart of the longer sutra; they call Amitabha's name, Namu Amida Butsu in Japan or Namo Amituofo in China, trusting that the vow has already been fulfilled.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the monk Dharmakara, who tied his own awakening to everyone else's. Your line: forty-eight vows.

Of all Dharmakara's vows, which one is the door? Tradition says Pure Land teachers in China and Japan kept circling back to a single vow and gave it a name of its own: the original vow, the root vow, in English often the primal vow. It doesn't describe jeweled trees or lotus ponds; other vows do that. It answers a plainer question, the one anybody would ask about a wonderful place far away. Who gets in?
screen: `WHICH VOW IS THE DOOR?` → `WHO GETS IN?` → `THE PRIMAL VOW.`

segments.voice: First, the words, in paraphrase. When I become a Buddha, if beings anywhere in the ten directions entrust themselves to me sincerely and joyfully, wish to be born in my land, and call my name, even ten times, and are not born there, may I not attain perfect awakening. Same shape as yesterday: if not, not me. Second, what it asks, and what it doesn't. Not years on the cushion, a library of sutras, a monastery, money, or a spotless past. Entrusting, wishing, and the name. The door is set low on purpose. A nurse finishing a night shift can walk through it. So can someone who never learned to read. You met this door already with Honen and Shinran. Third, the hard clause. The vow ends with an exception: those who commit the gravest wrongs and slander the teaching. Pure Land teachers have wrestled with that line. Some read it as a warning meant to keep people from those harms, more than a locked gate. Japanese schools that grew from this vow read it in their own ways, and the coming days will meet them. Fourth, why primal. In Japanese the word is hongan, the original, root vow. The other vows describe the land; this one opens it. And since the sutra says Dharmakara became a Buddha, Pure Land teachers read the vow as already fulfilled. In their telling, the door isn't about to open. It's open.
screen: `THE WORDS OF THE VOW.` · `WHAT IT ASKS, AND WHAT IT DOESN'T.` · `THE HARD CLAUSE.` · `THE DOOR IS ALREADY OPEN.` · then, large: `THE PRIMAL VOW.`

segments.voice: Pure Land Buddhists in Japan say Namu Amida Butsu; in China, Namo Amituofo. If this is your practice, say the name once, slowly and sincerely, and rest; if not, just listen to its sound in your mind, like a neighbor's song through a wall. Either way, let the breath slow, and stay with the picture of a door offered, not earned.

Your line: the door is open: trust and the name. No learning, money or spotless past required. That's today.

1258.title: Amitabha
1258.hook: Buddha of Infinite Light and Infinite Life
1258.howItsDone: Pure Land Buddhists keep images of Amitabha, seated or standing with one hand lowered in welcome, on temple and home altars, and call his name as Namu Amida Butsu in Japan or Namo Amituofo in China.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the primal vow: entrusting, wishing, the name, and a door the sutra says is already open. Your line: the primal vow.

A gilded figure seated on a temple altar in Japan, hands in the lap, fingers and thumbs forming two small circles. A tall standing figure in a Chinese hall, one hand raised, the other lowered and open, as if reaching down to someone. A small paper image taped above a bed in a nursing home. Three images, one Buddha. In Japan he's Amida. In China, Amituofo. In the Sanskrit sutras he carries two names, and today's word is the first: Amitabha.
screen: `A SEATED FIGURE IN JAPAN.` → `A HAND REACHING DOWN.` → `AMITABHA.`

segments.voice: First, the two names, which the short sutra explains itself. You heard part of this with Honen; here's the whole. Why is that Buddha called Amitabha? Because his light is measureless, shining without obstruction over the Buddha-lands in every direction. And why Amitayus? Because his life, and the life of the people in his land, is measureless too. Amitabha, infinite light. Amitayus, infinite life. The Japanese Amida holds both. Second, who he is: the monk from two days ago. The longer sutra says Dharmakara kept his vows, became a Buddha, and lives now in the land of bliss. So every time someone says his name, they name a vow kept. Third, the light: without obstruction. Sunlight on a city doesn't pick which roofs to land on, and in the sutra Amitabha's light reaches every land, near and far. One clarification, since the shops confuse it: Amitabha isn't the laughing, round-bellied figure in gift shops. That's Budai, Hotei in Japan, a different figure altogether. Fourth, how people meet him: through images like these, through the name in Japanese, Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese, and, the short sutra says, at the end of life, when he appears with a holy company before a dying person who has held his name in mind. Some readers see that welcome in the standing statue's lowered hand.
screen: `TWO NAMES: LIGHT AND LIFE.` · `DHARMAKARA, A VOW KEPT.` · `LIGHT WITHOUT OBSTRUCTION.` · `THE HAND REACHING DOWN.` · then, large: `INFINITE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Picture a small, warm light in the center of your chest, the size of a candle flame, and with each out-breath let it grow: your body, the room, the street, the city. Let it spread until it has no edge and nothing blocks it, not walls, not distance, not anyone's past, and rest there, breathing.

1259.title: The land described
1259.hook: jeweled trees, lotus ponds, birds whose songs are the teaching (Smaller Sukhavati-vyuha)
1259.howItsDone: Pure Land Buddhists chant the short sutra on the land of bliss in their services, and its pictures of lotus ponds, jeweled trees and singing birds appear in temple paintings and altar decorations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Amitabha: infinite light, infinite life, and a hand reaching down. Your line: infinite light.

Listen before you look. When the short sutra describes the land of bliss, it fills it with sound. Music drifts down from the sky. A breeze moves through rows of jeweled trees, and they ring. And there are birds, swans, peacocks, parrots and others, singing by day and by night. The Buddha tells Shariputra what they're singing, and it isn't only birdsong. The sutra lingers over every pond and branch. Today: the land described.
screen: `MUSIC FROM THE SKY.` → `TREES THAT RING.` → `THE LAND DESCRIBED.`

segments.voice: Begin with the water. The land has lotus ponds of jewels, the sutra says, with clear water and golden sand covering the bottom. The lotuses are as large as cart wheels, and each shines with the light of its own color: blue with blue light, yellow with yellow, red with red, white with white. Next, the trees and the sky. Rows of jeweled trees line the paths, hung with nets of bells, and when the breeze moves them, they sound like many instruments playing together. Flowers fall from the sky. In the early morning, the people there gather them in their robes, carry them off to offer to Buddhas in other worlds, and come home in time for their meal. Then the birds. What they sing is the teaching: the qualities and practices that lead to awakening, the path itself, in birdsong. Anyone who hears them begins to remember the Buddha, the teaching and the community. Last, the turn. The Buddha tells Shariputra not to imagine these birds were born as birds because of past wrongdoing. In that land, he says, the lower realms don't exist, not even as a name. Amitabha made the birds himself, so their songs would carry the teaching. Nothing there is just scenery. The water, the trees, the bells and the birds are all teachers.
screen: `LOTUSES SHINING THEIR OWN COLOR.` · `TREES THAT RING IN THE BREEZE.` · `BIRDS SINGING THE TEACHING.` · `NO BIRD THERE FOR PAST WRONGS.` · then, large: `THE BIRDS TEACH.`

segments.voice: If you can, open a window or step outside and listen for birds; if there are none, listen to whatever is there, a fan, traffic, rain, a neighbor's radio. Don't name or judge the sounds; let each arrive the way the sutra's birds do, as if saying something simple: this, now, wake up. When the mind wanders, let the next sound bring you back.
The land described: lotus ponds shining in their own colors, jeweled trees that ring in the breeze, flowers from the sky, and birds whose songs are the teaching. Today's word.
Your line: the birds teach. Even the lotuses shine with their own light. Twelve fifty-nine, done.

1260.title: Queen Vaidehi
1260.hook: imprisoned by her son Ajatasattu, the queen asks for a land without sorrow (Amitayur-dhyana, Takakusu)
1260.howItsDone: The sutra that opens with Vaidehi's story, the Amitayur-dhyana or meditation sutra, is chanted and studied in Chinese and Japanese Pure Land communities alongside the two sutras on the land of bliss.

segments.voice: The week closes. Zen ended on just sit. Then a new land: Sukhavati, the land of bliss. A monk's forty-eight vows. The primal vow. Amitabha's infinite light. And yesterday, a land where the birds teach.
screen: `JUST SIT.` · `THE LAND OF BLISS.` · `INFINITE LIGHT.` · `THE BIRDS TEACH.`

segments.voice: A prison inside a palace. King Bimbisara, a follower of the Buddha, has been locked away by his own son, Prince Ajatasattu, who means to let him starve. Nobody may bring him food. But every day the queen visits. First she bathes, covers her body with a paste of honey and flour, and hides juice inside her jewelry. Behind the locked door, in secret, the king eats. Day after day, he lives. Her story opens a sutra, and her name is today's word: Queen Vaidehi.
screen: `A PRISON INSIDE A PALACE.` → `HONEY, FLOUR, HIDDEN JUICE.` → `QUEEN VAIDEHI.`

segments.voice: First, the discovery. The prince learns his father is still alive, and why. He draws his sword against his own mother. His ministers stop him, warning that killing her would be a crime beyond anything a king should do. So he doesn't kill her; he locks her away too. Second, the cry. Alone and grieving, Vaidehi turns toward Vulture Peak, where the Buddha is staying, bows, and asks for help. The Buddha comes. She throws herself down in tears: what did I do to have a son like this? Then she asks for something larger than rescue. Show me a land without sorrow and trouble, where I can be born. I don't want this world anymore. Third, the answer. The sutra says light streams from between the Buddha's brows, and in it appear the lands of the Buddhas, one after another. She looks at them all, and chooses the land of Amitabha. Then she asks the question the rest of the sutra answers: how do I see it? Fourth, who receives this teaching. Not a monk on a mountain, not a scholar in a hall. A mother and a wife, locked in a room after the worst day of her life. Some Pure Land teachers read Vaidehi as an ordinary person, the kind the teaching was always meant for. The meditations that follow are given to grief, because grief asked.
screen: `THE SWORD, AND THE LOCKED ROOM.` · `A CRY TOWARD VULTURE PEAK.` · `LANDS SHOWN IN A RAY OF LIGHT.` · `A TEACHING GIVEN TO GRIEF.` · then, large: `A LAND WITHOUT SORROW.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person carrying sorrow right now, a friend, a parent, someone in the news, maybe yourself, and see their face clearly. Breathe in and notice their sorrow without fixing it; breathe out and silently wish them free of it, in plain words of your own, one breath at a time, the way metta practice does. And if the sorrow is yours and you don't want to be alive, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Queen Vaidehi. The imprisoned queen of the meditation sutra, who asked the Buddha for a land without sorrow and chose the land of Amitabha. Today's word.
Your line: a land without sorrow. Her next question was how to see it. That's the week, done.

chat.says: Why does a Pure Land sutra begin with a queen locked in a room?

To show that only royalty could hear the Pure Land teaching then.
To show the Buddha only teaches people who come to him calm.
